video_title: Nate Silver: Democrats Have a 75% Shot at the Senate

If I were donating money I'd focus more on those races where where there's not wall-to-wall media coverage. We're asking you to you know, the the future The easiest way to predict the future is to make it and we have 14 days to make it but recognizing you get deserve some grace. Sitting here on October the 22nd, what do you what are your predictions or what are you seeing with respect to the midterms? >> So, I'd be precise and say that we make probabilistic forecasts and not and not predictions. Polls can be off in either direction. Um but as of when we're recording this in late October Democrats, I'll just use round numbers, have around a 75% chance to win the Senate. That's been trending upwards since Labor Day and about 95% >> It's up to seven It's up to three and four to take the Senate now? >> That's what our model says and I think it's a good model. Um you know, one should keep in mind that in our model Hillary Clinton's chances were also around 70% and I in 2016 other models had her higher, so we're often more cautious. But I mean I I I put it like this, every sign except one would point toward it being a good Democratic year. And those signs include President Trump having some of the worst approval ratings ever at a midterm. They include, you know, gas being $4.30 a gallon and as of when we're recording this, maybe going up again. They include the long history of the president's party losing a bunch of seats at the midterms. Um The only thing that and they include like lots of signs of Democratic enthusiasm in the early vote, Democrats are turning out their regular voters. We'll see if Republicans are able to do that. The only thing going against Democrats is that the most important races are being conducted in very red territory. So, um you know, if Democrats were to win in purple North Carolina and blue Maine, although Susan Collins has been tough to defeat in the past, that would net them only two seats when they need four. So, they have to win a state or multiple states in fact that Trump won by double digits in 2024. Texas, Ohio, Iowa, Alaska, Kansas is the main part of the menu, maybe Nebraska a little bit. The House is different. The House you'd have to have a profound surprising polling error, um bigger than we saw in 2016 or the other Trump elections. Um I think in the house you might get some candidates who have been in a bunch of purple or slightly red cycles who are not prepared for for a very high Democratic turnout or a very depressed Republican turnout. I mean that would be what would worry me if I were President Trump, right? Trump benefited in 2024 from irregular voters turning out. Um we saw for example in South Texas a big working-class Hispanic vote, right? We saw young men of all races and ethnicities kind of voting for Trump for the first time in 2024. Those are not groups that typically turn out very much at midterms and this kind of magical power that Trump has to get voters to walk on glass to vote for him who might be irregular voters otherwise has never really carried over to the midterms or to other types of elections in the Trump era. Um Combine with the fact that you have some less than compelling Republican candidates, you know, Ken Paxton I think won't motivate the same type of passion from voters that that Trump might. People are talking about a blue wave and then other people say it's not a wave, it's a rip tide. And when you see some of these self-inflicted injuries like the one we're seeing or we saw with Vivek Ramaswamy in Ohio, do you think it's a case that we have actually pretty good Democratic candidates on the ballot this time or the people Is it a blue tsunami or a red rip tide in your view? I think the rip tide argument is cope. I mean the polls can be wrong. But the polls are pretty clear that Democrats are are If the polls are right, Democrats will have a pretty good year. Um I keep people in mind too that we had a previous midterm under Trump in 2018 and Democrats won the popular vote for the US House by eight and a half points. They flipped 40 or 41 or 42 something House seats. Um They lost a couple of Senate seats cuz they were conducted in very red territory like North Dakota where they had an incumbent so you could argue that's a ominous precedent for the Senate. Um but we kind of know that like >> [laughter] >> when you have a lame duck second-term president, when consumers are very concerned about the cost of living and gas in particular, I mean anytime, you know, it's a catchphrase, but like anytime you drive by gas station, it's kind of an advertisement for the Democratic Party, basically. If you treated every race as an independent coin flip, it would be 90% but when you account for the fact that you can have these correlated errors either regionally or nationally, like you saw in a couple of the really all three of the Trump presidential years, that's kind of where the GOP hopes of salvaging the situation in the in the Senate come in. >> How do you apply this? I think they kind of have to move quickly and I think they have to um use AI tools not to cheat with, but as like you know, as productivity aids. I think we're in a window right now where um there is still a benefit from early adoption, right? In my case, um we program these models. Well, now all of a sudden in Claude and ChatGPT, you know, I have a couple of expert programmers that work very quickly. They're not great at model design, they're not great at the empirical questions, but in terms of like can you audit my code, update the code, make this program run 10 times faster, right? They're very helpful with that. >> And when you start these things, do you take outside capital or do you self-finance them? And generally, what does the team look like? How many people front of mic, behind mic, and what do they do? >> So, for Silver Bulletin, we have four people counting myself, and um we've never had to raise capital. The The reason being that I mean, so it does help to have obviously an established name, so the the kind of day well, 3 months after my last day at Disney, you know, we started adding paid subscriptions, and so it's always been a a cash flow positive business. One nice thing about newsletters is that you're, you know, if someone subscribes on October 22nd, then they'll pay for the whole month or the whole year then, and so yeah, I I you know, I think I've avoided what I think can be the trap of like of like raising money and feeling like I had some obligation to spend it, right? Because like I, you know, I'm one of those people where I don't like having more than two appointments in a day on my on my calendar, right? I I need time and space creatively for um for writing, for for building models, um for things like that, and so I I'm quite happy with this with the smaller team. I mean, I we think more likely than not we'll do some hiring before 2028, but yeah, look, I think especially in a world where you're able to lift up some of the things that are more difficult like, you know, for example, AI is also good at copy editing, right? >> Mhm. >> So, instead of having to hire a copy editor, then Claude or GPT can do it, and like that helps a little bit. But yeah, to have you know, a team of a half dozen really dedicated people. I don't know if that's the future of industry in general, but that that works well for for my lifestyle and and my business goals. >> Time and space to be creative. Nate Silver is a statistician, political analyst, and New York Times best-selling author of The Signal and the Noise and On the Edge.
